en: The Sūtra on the Brahmin Girl Śirīṣā Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of the rishis.
He turned the wheel of Dharma together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and countless bodhisattvas, who had gathered from various different buddha-fields.
At that time, at dawn, the World-Honored One adjusted his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to bestow blessings upon all.

The worthy Ānanda attended him according to the usual protocol, and the Great Sage entered the great city of Vārāṇasī, proceeding through the streets and alleys until he reached the gate of a brahmin.

That brahmin had a daughter named Śyāmāvatī; from afar she beheld the Buddha’s body—exquisite, sublime, and majestic in its spiritual power—and saw that his mind was serene, his faculties were tranquil, he maintained supreme, profound silence and the highest detachment, free from decline and with all fear forever eliminated.

His mind was pure and free from defilement, like a great, limpid abyss; his purple-golden complexion shone like a mountain of jewels; he was as if filled with celestial trees bearing abundant flowers and fruit; his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the eighty minor marks were spread throughout his form.

It was as radiant as a great hall with its precious pillars; it stood loftily and preeminently like Mount Sumeru; it was as bright as the full moon among the multitude of stars; and it was as dazzling and brilliant as the rising sun, illuminating everything without exception.

Seeing the Buddha approaching and standing outside the gate, the woman’s heart leaped with joy; she turned back to prepare a seat, then returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, knelt for a long time, and said: “Welcome!
"Please remain; we pray that the Holy One will deign to grace us with his presence.
The Buddha, moved by compassion, entered the hall and took his seat.
Śreṇika was filled with joy and, bowing his head repeatedly, took a small stool to sit before the Buddha, whereupon he addressed him, saying:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!

We have heard that the Tathāgata once traveled to the Deer Park of the Seers at Vārāṇasī, where, for the sake of śramaṇas, brahmins, Brahmās, nāgas, spirits, Māras, worldlings, and all classes of sentient beings, he turned the unsurpassed wheel and caused the True Dharma to flourish.”
The Buddha told the Brahmānī: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is exactly as you have said; I travel through this land, turning the unsurpassed wheel and proclaiming the True Dharma for those who have not yet heard it, never employing what is not the Dharma.
Then Śrīgupta asked the Buddha, "What is meant by the Wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata?"
The World-Honored One told the woman:
"I turn the wheel of Dharma by means of the twelvefold dependent origination.
Śrīmatī addressed the Buddha:

“Out of your great kindness, please further analyze and explain for me in detail the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, so that I may understand the ultimate destination of the Wheel of Dharma and its underlying meaning.
The Buddha said,
“Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain its meaning for you.
The Brahmin maiden Śuci accepted the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said to her:

"If one calculates that there is a self, then there is beginning and end; arising from non-arising, conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact, there is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving, there is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping, there is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming, birth (*jāti*) comes to pass; and conditioned by birth, old age, sickness, death, suffering, lamentation, and despair arise—the great mass of afflictions assembles."
“In this way, daughter!

With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of consciousness, volitional formations, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and great suffering; all these afflictions are completely eliminated.”

If you wish to know, it is because of this Dharma that, at the Deer Park of the Sages in Vārāṇasī, I have turned the wheel of the Dharma for the sake of śramaṇas, brahmins, Brahmās, nāgas, spirits, Māras, and the people of the world, explaining the twelve links of dependent origination; if one receives and practices it, one may thereby attain deliverance.
Śūramati asked the Buddha, “Indeed,
O God among Gods, does the Dharma have an interior or an exterior?
The Buddha addressed the woman, saying:
"No," the woman asked again,
"Does the Dharma perhaps abide by the name 'ignorance'?"
He replied, "No. The woman asked again:
“Is there, then, any arising of clarity or any cessation? He replied, “No!”
The woman asked again:
"Does that one who is enlightened and penetrating possess any physical form or appearance?
He replied:
"No," she replied.
The woman asked again,
"By what causes and conditions is this body brought about?"
"Since there is no delusion, from what could birth arise?
One gives rise to a mind of pride and conceit, thereby forming one's conduct; what are the causes and conditions by which these are brought together?
He spoke again:
"O Great Sage! If a tree has no root, by what cause could its trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit suddenly arise?
It is even so, World-Honored One!"
Considering that ignorance has no form or image, if it arises from conditions and leads to arrogance, what is the source of this lack of wisdom that results in volitional action?
"From what cause does this assembly of manifold afflictions arise?
The Buddha told the woman:
"If you wish to know the various characteristics, they are fundamentally and entirely pure; it is also thus."

Regarding the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), a phenomenon does not know a phenomenon; yet foolish, ignorant worldlings, having heard neither of sin nor merit, create danger and peril. Because of this danger and peril, there is beginning and end; because of beginning and end, there is suffering and pleasure.

When one understands this, there is neither the commission of sin nor the accumulation of merit; furthermore, there is no advancing or retreating, no beginning or end, and no encountering of suffering or meeting with joy.
The Buddha told Shouyi:
"If you wish to know, it is like a conjurer who creates an emanation; that emanated person does not think or say:
'I am an emanation.'"
That illusionist may take the real for the unreal, or the unreal for the real; all such things are deceptive, fraudulent, foolish, and false methods.
When one calculates this illusionist and the person created by him, there is neither a creator nor a creation; they too are empty, hollow, delusive, bewildering, and ignorant methods.
"What do you think?
Does that which is a magical illusion have an interior or an exterior?
He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! What do you think?"
"Since illusion has no abiding place, how could it have a name such as 'self'? He replied, "No!"
"O God among Gods!
What do you think?
Does that which is an illusory transformation ever go to a future life and return again?"
He replied, “No, O God among Gods!”
"What do you think?
Does that illusion have anything that arises or anything that ceases?
He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! What do you think?"
"How could that which is an illusion have any substantial form or appearance? He replied, "No!"
“O God among Gods!
What do you think? Does that which is a magical illusion have seeing or hearing, or does it have illusion or non-illusion?”
He replied: “No, O God among Gods!”
The woman said to the Buddha:
“I have heard it said that for one who is a magical creation, there is neither seeing nor hearing of whether there is illusion or no illusion.
The World-Honored One asked again:
"What do you think?
If that illusory being were without a body, could it possibly cause the illusory being to initiate various magical arts?
The woman replied:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
That which is an illusory transformation is truly thus: it is genuinely non-existent.
The Buddha spoke again:
"So it is! So it is! Daughter!"

That ignorance has neither interior nor exterior; when one examines its phenomena, they likewise do not exist, nor do they possess names. That ignorance does not reach a future life, nor does it return; that ignorance neither arises nor ceases, and that ignorance has no form or image.

Driven by the conditions of ignorance, there arise volitional formations; from these come name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, sickness, death, suffering, grief, and despair—the great mass of afflictions thus assembles.
At that time, the girl Śirī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This is truly marvelous!
It is most unprecedented!”
That which the World-Honored One has manifested is unattainable. Why is this?
Because the Buddha is the God among Gods!

In the midst of space, he turns the wheel of Dharma: the inconceivable wheel of Dharma, the immeasurable and limitless wheel of Dharma, the wheel of Dharma that is unattainable, the formless wheel of Dharma, the non-arising wheel of Dharma, and the wheel of Dharma of parinirvāṇa.
The World-Honored One said: "So it is! So it is!"

It is exactly as you have said: the wheel I turn is the wheel of emptiness; the wheel of Dharma I turn is inconceivable, the wheel of Dharma I turn is beyond measure. This wheel that can be turned is immeasurable and without attainment, formless and unarisen, for the sake of parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the maiden Śirīṣā was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a virtuous mind arose within her, and she offered powdered sandalwood incense and various floral perfumes, scattering them over the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
By means of these roots of virtue, they vow to provide protection and skillfully rescue and gather [beings].

They subdue the sense faculties and restrain craving and desire; they attain the turning of the Wheel of Dharma—the wheel of emptiness and non-existence, the inconceivable wheel that is beyond measure or limit.
"Immeasurable and unattainable, formless and unborn—this is the wheel of parinirvāṇa.

The Buddha then rejoiced, and five-colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and green—issued forth from his mouth. This great radiance shone universally throughout the countless buddha-lands of the ten directions, completely eclipsing the brilliance of the sun and moon; it then returned, circled the Buddha’s body three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
The worthy Ānanda was proficient in seven dharmas:
first, knowing the meaning;
second, understanding the teachings.
Third is the awakening of time;
fourth is the understanding of seasons;
fifth is the clarity regarding the assembly.
Sixth, to refine oneself;
seventh, to discern the fundamental nature of others.
Thereupon, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Now that the Great Sage is filled with joy and desire, what is the cause of this response? We pray that you will explain its meaning.
Indeed, O God among Gods!
Out of great compassion and for the sake of great peace and security, please take pity on the devas and the people of the world, and explain it to us in detail."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Did you see the Brahmā maiden Śīlavatī making offerings to the Buddha by scattering powdered sandalwood, flowers, perfumes, and incense?”
With his heart, he made a vow to attain the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
He replied, “I have seen it.”
The Buddha said:

"This girl, by means of these roots of merit, shall protect herself and bring peace to others, providing extensive rescue and guidance. After the end of her life, she shall transform her female body; for eighty-four billion kalpas, she shall not fall into the evil realms. She shall make offerings to sixty thousand Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, leave the household life to pursue the Way, resolve upon the state of a śramaṇa, and listen to and receive the sūtras and the Dharma."

Having received the Dharma of the sutras, they immediately recited them, upholding the True Dharma of the Tathāgata while he was present; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they made offerings to his relics and exhorted and transformed countless, immeasurable beings beyond calculation, establishing them in the unsurpassed, true, and right path. Finally, at the end of the kalpa in a future age, within this trichiliocosm, they shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment. That kalpa shall be named Ratnaprabhāsa (Jewel Radiance), and the Buddha shall be named Ratnarcis Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall be a full kalpa; for the sake of immeasurable multitudes of beings, he shall exhort them toward the Way and cause their merit to increase, until finally, in the realm of nirvana without remainder, he attains parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Under which Buddha did this maiden Śubhāmatī plant the roots of all virtues?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, this woman first resolved her mind upon the Way while in her female body, taking precious pearls and necklaces to scatter over the Buddha.
Having come before me again in this present life, her aspiration is for the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way."

He also conceived a heart of joy toward Śikhi Buddha, the Tathāgata and Perfectly Awakened One, and with profound faith, he removed his garment and offered it to the Buddha. Out of his family’s faith, he left the household life to become a monk; for a full thousand years, he purely cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) and repeatedly inquired about the profound and wondrous Dharma.

During the time of the Tathāgata Anupamapatra, he made offerings to the World-Honored One and his disciples on the fifteenth day of the month, providing them with everything in full abundance, and likewise resolved his will upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

During the time of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Perfectly Awakened One, he delighted in the study of the Dharma and committed its verses and phrases to memory; he scattered various pearls and famous incenses upon the Buddha and made a vow in his heart to attain perfect awakening himself.

During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kanakamuni Buddha, he anointed a stupa with incense for the duration of his life, and provided offerings of clothing, food and drink, medicine, and bedding; furthermore, for two days, he made offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of noble disciples.
Having seen Kāśyapa Buddha, she made offerings and served him without abandoning her resolve for the Way.
Now, by making offerings to me, she shall transform her female body and thereafter attain the Buddha-way to deliver sentient beings.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all were filled with joy.
This is the *Sūtra on the Brahmin Girl Śrīmatī* as taught by the Buddha.
